demographics.trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another

vignette: The collision happens on a Tuesday in November, the kind of morning that begins with gray skies and ends with silence. Arjun glances down at his phone for one second to confirm the street name. When he looks up, the cyclist is already drifting wide around a parked delivery truck. His foot slams the brake. The van's tires lose traction on the wet asphalt. The world collapses into the sound of bending metal and a sharp, wet thud. His hands freeze on the wheel. His breath stops. Through the windshield, he watches a man's body slide beneath a fender, then stills. The turn signal clicks. Click. Click. Click. The rhythm of his own panic. In the hours that follow, sirens wail and orange vests move with practiced urgency. Arjun stands on the sidewalk, rain soaking through his jacket, watching paramedics lift a stretcher. No one tells him he is legally at fault, but the weight settles in his ribs anyway, heavy and permanent. He signs the police reports. He calls his wife, Meera, and tells her he will be late. His voice stays steady until he hangs up. Then he sits in the idling van for two hours, staring at his reflection in the cracked side mirror, unable to turn the key. Now, at thirty-four, Arjun still drives the route, but the city has shrunk. He wakes before his alarm, his heart hammering against his ribs, convinced he hears the screech of tires in the space between dreams. When he closes his eyes, he sees the man's helmet crack. He sees the ambulance lights painting their apartment ceiling. He stops sleeping with his feet under the covers; he keeps them on the floor, ready to run, though there is nothing to flee. The guilt does not sound like a voice. It sounds like the quiet hum of his own pulse, relentless, reminding him of what he broke. He checks the side mirrors twice before turning the engine. His knuckles stay white. When a car backfires three streets over, his shoulders jump to his ears. He exhales slowly, forcing his jaw to unclench. He has mapped a wide, sunlit circle around the intersection where the man fell. He avoids evening shifts. He avoids the smell of burnt rubber. When his dispatch app pings with an address in that zone, he stares at the screen until it goes dark. He reroutes. He always reroutes. The extra miles stack up in his head like unpaid debts. Meera has learned not to ask about the route. She notices the way he flinches when dishes clatter in the sink, the way he scans the street from their balcony. His parents' quiet expectations of South Asian men to bear hardship without complaint sit heavy in his chest, but he carries it alone. He used to take pride in the rhythm of the city, the satisfaction of a full manifest, the ability to provide without complaint. Now, every turn feels like a gamble. He drives like he is walking on ice, even when the pavement is dry. He pulls away from the curb, tires whispering against the damp road. A pedestrian steps off the sidewalk. Arjun's foot hovers over the brake. His chest tightens. He reminds himself of the distance, of the clear line of sight, of the way his hands now grip the wheel with deliberate, careful pressure. The delivery app chimes. He unlocks the door. He puts the van in gear. The city moves around him, loud and indifferent, but he sits inside his own quiet storm, waiting for the light to change.
